entries.title: White Sox' rotation in flux for rest of Cubs series
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox’ pitching staff is in dire need of a day off.</p><p>But with a makeup game Thursday against the Braves replacing a day off, the Sox won’t get a breather until Aug. 27. After taxing their bulk and high-leverage relievers during a three-game sweep of the Tigers, the Sox will piece together a pitching plan for the rest of the Cubs series.</p><p>“It’ll be day by day here,” manager Will Venable said before the series opener Monday at Wrigley Field. “We’re going to figure out where we’re at after today. We have some availability limitations in our bullpen that can impact some things.”</p><p>Those limitations are from Sean Newcomb pitching the last 2 ⅓ innings Sunday in Detroit after he opened the series with 1 ⅓ innings Friday, and Grant Taylor and Bryan Hudson pitching at least an inning each on Friday and Saturday.</p><p>The Sox pulled off the sweep despite using a bullpen game Friday and getting only 5 ⅓ innings from Anthony Kay on Saturday and 4 ⅓ from Sean Burke on Sunday. They followed Venable’s mantra of winning today and worrying about tomorrow later.</p><p>“That’s generally the way you go about it,” he said. “Obviously, we have to be mindful of what it means for the future. But the priority is to win the game today. So that’s the approach and why we’re not going to be making decisions on our starters for the rest of this series.”</p><p>Venable went into Game 1 hoping for a lengthy start from Luis Castillo, who gave the Sox just that last week in his second start for them. He pitched seven scoreless innings against the Reds, allowing one hit and striking out a season-high 10.</p><p>One pitcher who didn’t throw against the Tigers is Erick Fedde, whom the Sox moved to the bullpen about two weeks ago. As long as he’s not needed in the opener against the Cubs, he’s an option to start Tuesday or Wednesday. The same holds true for Jose Urquidy, who pitched 3 ⅔ innings in the bullpen game against the Tigers.</p><p>“I really don’t know,” Venable said. “We really are day-to-day here with this, just because of the usage we have had over this last series. So we’ll reserve our plan for after the game.”</p><h3>Teel nearing rehab</h3><p>Injured catcher Kyle Teel is a week or two away from yet another rehab assignment, this time for the sprained left ankle he suffered July 20 against the Rangers. He took batting practice Monday at Wrigley.</p><p>“We still don’t have a definite timeline,” Venable said. “We have to see how he’s feeling and how he recovers after the hitting. The most important thing is going to be the running and how he responds to that.”</p><p>Teel has been running for a couple of weeks, topping out at what Venable said was 80% speed. Whenever he returns, the Sox will have another decision to make at catcher, where they just added veteran Jake Rogers on Saturday.</p><h3>Colson gets a break</h3><p>Venable gave shortstop Colson Montgomery the day off, saying it was his turn for a break.</p><p>“He’s fine,” Venable said. “We talked about getting these guys days [off]. He was the one guy that was running hot for us. So I just wanted to give him a day.”</p><p>The timing was curious. Montgomery appeared to be coming out of a funk, going 3-for-8 with a double and three RBI in his last two games. Also, in his career against Cubs lefty Shota Imanaga, who started Monday, the lefty-hitting Montgomery is 1-for-2 with a homer</p><h3>Broadcast news</h3><p>Prime Video agreed to make Chicago Sports entries.title: Cubs and Sox fans swarm Wrigley Field for Crosstown Classic
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of baseball fans swarmed Wrigley Field Monday for one of the most highly anticipated games of the year — the Cubs vs. the White Sox in the Crosstown Classic.</p><p>Fans wore Cubs or Sox gear, repping their preferred Chicago team. But a few couldn’t decide which one to choose.</p><p>“I am a Chicago fan, but when they play each other I can’t decide who to root for,” said Kenneth McGhee, wearing a jersey split in half with one side for the Cubs and the other for the Sox.</p><p>Fans came from all over Chicago and beyond to experience the rivalry. Mark Yolkowski and his son, Hudson Yolkowski, had a layover in Chicago on their way from Toronto to Minnesota, so they walked around outside Wrigley Field.</p><p>“The vibe is unreal, it’s quite the scene,” Mark Yolkowski said. “Cubs fans, Sox fans, you can tell the battle of Chicago, it’s something to be a part of, something to witness.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Jeanie Buss will fight siblings' plan to sell Lakers minority ownership stake to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — Los Angeles Lakers governor Jeanie Buss is legally contesting her siblings' plan to sell the family's remaining 17.8% minority ownership stake in the team to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, according to a letter obtained Monday by The Associated Press.</p><p>ESPN and The Athletic first reported that the siblings had voted to sell the family trust's remaining interest in the 17-time NBA champion team purchased by their father, Jerry Buss, in 1979. The decision would end Jeanie Buss' tenure as the Lakers' governor because that job requires at least 15% ownership of the team.</p><p>Jeanie Buss' attorney, Adam Streisand, wrote to representatives for her five siblings to state that any decision to sell the family trust's ownership stake could not be "effectuated without approval of the current co-trustees, Jeanie, Janie and Joey Buss."</p><p>The letter further states that the co-trustees "are bound to vote the Los Angeles Lakers, Inc. shares to ensure that the minimum 15% ownership requirement is maintained in order to ensure that Jeanie Buss may remain Controlling Owner. Any attempt by the co-trustees to do otherwise, and any attempt to aid or abet the co-trustees as such, would constitute a breach of trust, breach of fiduciary duty and be in contempt of court."</p><p>Jeanie Buss has been the Lakers' governor since Jerry Buss' death in 2013, and she led the family's decision to sell a controlling stake in the Lakers to Dodgers owner Mark Walter last year at a valuation of $10 billion. Walter, who is under federal investigation for tax issues, abruptly reached a deal earlier this month to flip the Lakers to Kushner and Iger at a valuation of $12.5 billion, another record for a pro sports team.</p><p>Venture capitalist Kushner and former Disney CEO Iger are reportedly buying about 65% of the team from Walter. They would own about 83% if they reach a deal with the Buss siblings — and Jeanie Buss would lose the governor role that she had been slated to keep at least through 2030 under the deal with Walter.</p><p>The Buss siblings have been in frequent conflict since their father's death, with Jeanie firing Jim from his job as the Lakers' head of basketball operations in 2017, followed a week later by a lawsuit against her brothers amid an attempt by Jim and Johnny to oust Jeanie from her role as the Lakers' controlling owner.</p><p>Not all of the six Buss siblings were in favor of the sale to Walter, and Joey and Jesse were fired from their front-office jobs with the team last November.</p><p>The siblings say they voted this month to sell their family's remaining interest in the Lakers, but Jeanie Buss claims any vote is void. ESPN reported that Jeanie Buss was the only sibling who didn't support the final sale.</p><p>"We have decided as a family to sell the remaining Buss Family Trust shares to the Bob Iger group as part of the ongoing transaction," the Buss family said in a statement. "We love the Lakers, Laker fans and will continue to support Los Angeles, but it is time to use this opportunity to move on and exit gracefully while we still can."</p><p>In his letter, Streisand said Joey and Jesse Buss have leaked information to ESPN for many years "for the malicious purpose of doing harm to the Los Angeles Lakers so long as Dr. Buss's chosen successor, Jeanie Buss, carries out her father's wishes."</p><p>Jerry Buss was a chemist and real estate investor who bought the Lakers, the NHL's Los Angeles Kings and the Forum arena from Jack Kent Cooke for $67.5 million. The Lakers quickly entered a renaissance in which they became known for their flashy "Showtime" style of play while winning five NBA titles between 1980 and 1988 behind Magic Johnson and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.</p><p>While the NBA and professional sports became increasingly more corporate, the Lakers remained essentially a family business despite their massive profile and steady success. Jerry Buss and the Lakers have employed many of the basketball world's greatest players and coaches of the past five decades, and Kobe Bryant led the Lakers to five additional championships between 2000 and 2010 before LeBron James added the 17th in 2020.</p><p>The sale agreement with Kushner and Iger still must be approved by the NBA's board of governors, and the process could take months.<br></p>

entries.title: Crosstown begins with mutual love for Chicago contenders, but what if Cubs, White Sox meet in World Series?
entries.summary: <p>Crosstown in the thick of a playoff race is interesting enough.</p><p>Could you imagine Crosstown in October?</p><p>“Sign me up,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> skipper Craig Counsell said before the first of three games with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> on Monday at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Yeah, you can sign everybody in this baseball-mad town up for that one, an event that might be big enough to earn the Chicago flag a fifth star.</p><p>“Iconic,” said Sox fan Mary Beth Szorc of Chicago.</p><p>A lot would have to go right for that to happen this fall, and the Cubs will consider this August matchup less of a playoff preview and more of the latest turn of their schedule.</p><p>“It doesn’t matter who you’re playing,” Cubs left fielder Ian Happ said of this time of year, “the games are meaningful.”</p><p>No one’s biting on the fan-fueled rivalry talk inside the Cubs’ clubhouse, nor should they be expected to. Happ’s from Pittsburgh, after all. He didn’t grow up with this series circled on his calendar, ready to claim bragging rights from every other-side-of-town fan he ran into for a weekend.</p><p>The electricity always gets cranked to 11 with Crosstown, with fireworks on the field and off it. Just ask Michael Barrett and A.J. Pierzynski, or a host of others who have been involved in game-winning homers, dugout blow-ups, bat flips, manager ejections and dueling no-hit bids.</p><p>Earlier this season, Crosstown was the emotional setting for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/18/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-heckler-white-sox-fan-crosstown-rivalry-viral" >Pete Crow-Armstrong’s vulgar interaction with a heckling Sox fan</a> and Edgar Quero’s walk-off home run.</p><p>The scene shifted North on Monday, and immediately, more fireworks: Crow-Armstrong and Seiya Suzuki riled up Cubs fans with back-to-back homers in the first inning.</p><p>The pregame scene Monday was more giddy excitement over a couple good teams than contending fan bases at each other’s throats, perhaps the result of a midweek, back-to-school series rather than midsummer games following a daylong Clark Street bar crawl or all-day tailgating on the South Side.</p><p>“It’s nice to see both teams doing well, for once,” said Sox fan Sawyer Phillips of Antioch, here with Cubs season-ticket holder buddy Colin Wieska. “It’s been a while since both teams have had winning records at this point in the season. It’s cool to see.”</p><p>“It’s a lot of fun at home,” said Cubs fan Larry Johnson of Rockford, in attendance with his Sox-fan wife, Ashley, as they celebrated their wedding anniversary. “We’re always throwing jabs, typical stuff.”</p><p>These Chicago baseball fans were rejecting the stereotype, choosing love over hate.</p><p>Speaking of love, Szorc was married at Rate Field — she still calls it Comiskey — with Cubs-fan friend Jen Pierce in attendance.</p><p>“Thirty-five years of friendship,” Szorc said, “we’ve never fought about [Crosstown].”</p><p>But this one seems like it’s for a little more than just bragging rights.</p><p>The Cubs and Sox both have realistic playoff aspirations. Though the Cubs owned baseball’s fifth best record when they woke up Monday, it was the Sox in position for a first-round playoff bye, thanks to their status as the second-best division leader in a weak American League, with the Cubs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/13/cubs-nl-central-standings-brewers-playoffs-postseason-wild-card-matthew-boyd-kevin-gausman-nationals-shelby-miller-injury-rehab-assignment" >still attempting to chase down the Brewers</a> in the NL Central.</p><p>Even amid all the love, the Friendly Confines were only so friendly. Cubs fans booed Sox pitchers as they walked to the bullpen in the first inning, and Sox fans booed Crow-Armstrong as he came to the plate.</p><p>Signage outside Murphy’s Bleachers called the Sox “still second in Chicago,” technically true if you’re going by the win-loss numbers. But there was only one first-place team in Monday’s game, and it wasn’t the Cubs.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Crosstown comes to the North Side <a href="https://t.co/GnP3GuxX2x">pic.twitter.com/GnP3GuxX2x</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2089445773482057998?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>If these two teams meet again in 2026, you can forget the nitpicking, only one thing will matter: the first title in 10 years, or the first title in 21?</p><p>Those are Ron Santo and Sammy Sosa’s numbers, so maybe there’s some good mojo in the Cubs’ favor?</p><p>Wait, both those guys played for the Sox, too. More for Cubs and Sox fans to agree on.</p><p>Looks like it’s on the 2026 teams to stir up a little more drama and reignite the rivalry.</p><p>Maybe with a third act this October?</p><p>“I’m in for all the fun, everything,” Counsell said. “You want to hype it up? I’m in for all of it.”</p>

entries.title: Man chased by CPD Officer Krystal Rivera indicted on drug charges
entries.summary: <p>The man Chicago police Officer Krystal Rivera was chasing when she was fatally shot by her partner last year was indicted on charges of conspiring to traffic fentanyl and cocaine in Chicago, according to the U.S. Attorney’s office.</p><p>Rivera and Officer Carlos Baker chased Jaylin Arnold to a Chatham apartment in June 2025, where Baker fired his gun, striking and killing Rivera. Arnold pleaded guilty to gun and drug charges in relation to Rivera’s death and was sentenced to eight years in prison as part of the plea deal — a sentence Rivera’s mother Yolanda Rivera called “extremely severe.”</p><p> Arnold, 28, was indicted Thursday by a federal grand jury for drug trafficking allegedly carried out with four other men between January and June of 2025, according to the indictment.</p><p>Yolanda Rivera has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Baker and the Chicago Police Department, alleging that at the time he shot her daughter, Baker had been struggling to accept that Krystal Rivera had ended their romantic relationship. Baker had a lengthy disciplinary record with more than a dozen misconduct complaints, the Sun-Times and Illinois Answers Project found.</p><p>The lawsuit says Krystal Rivera threatened to tell his live-in girlfriend about their relationship, then broke up with him. The day before the shooting, Baker showed up uninvited at Krystal Rivera’s home, the lawsuit says.</p><p>After Arnold pleaded guilty to the drug and gun charges related to her daughter’s death, Yolanda Rivera said he “deserves a sentence that reflects the truth of their role — not the burden of institutional failures beyond his control.”</p><p>At the time of the plea, Arnold’s attorney, Michael Clancy, said it’s important not to conflate Arnold’s gun charges with Krystal Rivera’s death.</p><p>“I think everyone has to remember he was not charged with the death of the officer for having anything to do with causing the death of the officer,” he said.</p><p>After Baker fired a single shot that struck Krystal Rivera, he waited more than 90 seconds to render aid as she gasped for breath, according to the lawsuit and bodycam footage.</p><p>“The officer failed to render aid when it was critically needed,” Yolanda Rivera said in court when Arnold pleaded guilty. “It’s difficult to accept Arnold should bear the weight.”</p><p>Arnold was previously sentenced to seven years in prison after being convicted on gun charges in 2023, and has been sentenced to prison at least two other times for gun charges.</p><p>Clancy didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the indictment.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago Teachers Union sues Illinois Policy Institute for 'toxic' branding, 'defamatory' claims about audits
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Teachers Union is taking aim at the Illinois Policy Institute and its legal arm, claiming in a defamation lawsuit filed Monday that social media posts and articles bashing the union’s finances and its president Stacy Davis Gates — and branding the union “toxic” — are part of a “deliberate campaign” to harm the union’s reputation.</p><p>The CTU is framing the suit as Davis Gates “standing up to the multimillion dollar marketing firm, Illinois Policy Institute," the Liberty Justice Center and Austin Berg, the nonprofit’s marketing vice president. The law firm identifies itself as nonpartisan, but it is known for taking on a <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/about/the-janus-case/" target="_blank" ><u>high-profile conservative legal case</u></a> before the Supreme Court that undermined the power of labor unions.</p><p>“Falsely accusing a labor union of fraud, dishonest accounting, and misuse of funds strikes at the heart of the Union’s integrity, fitness, and ability to represent and advocate for its approximately 30,000 member-educators,” the suit, filed in Cook County Circuit Court, states.</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union is a political powerhouse, helping to elect Mayor Brandon Johnson and propelling preferred political candidates throughout the city. The suit comes ahead of crucial school board races in the November election — and as Johnson mulls another mayoral run. John Owen, attorney for the CTU, would not comment on the timing of the suit but pointed the finger at the defendants’ “ongoing campaign.”</p><p>“These statements, the first incidents we refer to, started in August of 2025. But that’s been an ongoing campaign to attack and smear the union,” Owen said. “And the union at this point has decided to stand up for itself and hold these defendants accountable for these defamatory statements.”</p><p>Most of what the suit calls defamatory statements relate to CTU audits that began in October 2024, when the Liberty Justice Center and four CTU members filed a suit claiming the union did not produce annual financial audit reports. That case is still pending in Cook County.</p><p>The CTU, which regularly slams the Trump administration, also in January received a letter from the U.S. Department of Labor informing the union of an audit of its annual financial report. That came after an inquiry by a Republican-led U.S. House committee last year. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/16/chicago-teachers-union-leaders-question-timing-of-second-federal-inquiry-into-finances" target="_blank" >Davis Gates said in an interview with WBEZ</a> that she believed the union was targeted politically because it “defends, protects, we expand the public good in ways that are oppositional to the right wing.” </p><p>The CTU has advocated for Black, transgender and immigrant students.</p><p>Debates about the transparency of the CTU’s finances date back to 2024 and stem from one member’s complaint that the union is withholding financial information from members. CTU officials in January provided WBEZ/Sun-Times with a sign-in sheet that showed one of that suit’s plaintiffs had viewed the union’s audit reports, which don’t include information about the CTU’s foundation. The CTU has <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/union/constitution/" target="_blank" ><u>insisted that its constitution</u></a> does not require the release of the full audits that also include the foundation’s finances.</p><p>The new lawsuit claims the finalization of the audit reports were delayed for “innocuous reasons,” including that the finalization for fiscal year 2020 through 2023 were delayed due to complications from the pandemic and staffing turnover, as well as the impact of a lawsuit to protect pension benefits. The suit says the reports have been available to CTU members for review.</p><p>The suit includes an Aug. 22, 2025, social media post by the Liberty Justice Center, which features a cartoon of Davis Gates and the words “Cooked Books,” mimicking the branding of the restaurant Cracker Barrel. The union says that post was “part of Defendant’s strategy to ‘make the union itself toxic’ through sustained negative messaging.” And the suit says the “cooked book” statement was defamatory because it “falsely imputed CTU’s engagement in criminal conduct.”</p><p>The union is also taking issue with several IPI statements, including a repeated label of the union as being “toxic,” which it called “a premeditated effort to hurt” the union.</p><p>The suit also takes aim at an IPI article from October 2025 that said the union is refusing to show its members the audits — saying the article omitted the “facts" regarding the availability of the audits and the reason for the timing delays. And it includes a social media post by the Liberty Justice Center in November 2025, featuring an AI-generated image of a cookbook called “Cooking The Books by Stacy Davis Gates and Jackson Potter,” referencing Davis Gates and the CTU vice president.</p><p>The suit claims that image is evidence of “actual malice” by the defendants and part of their “deliberate campaign to harm CTU’s reputation.”</p><p>The suit is seeking a judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, including compensatory damages, punitive damages, the costs of the suit and additional relief. It’s also seeking a jury trial.</p><p>The defendants did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.</p><p><i>Contributing: WBEZ education reporter Sarah Karp</i></p>

entries.title: White Sox-Cubs rivalry delivers at Wrigley, despite outcome for South Siders
entries.summary: <p>When Ozzie Guillen was managing the White Sox, he loathed coming to Wrigley Field and loved sharing his thoughts with the media. From the cramped quarters to the rats that he swore were bigger than pigs, Guillen had a comment for everything.</p><p>Before the crosstown-series opener Monday at Wrigley, second-year Sox manager Will Venable was asked if he harbors similar hostility toward the venerable ballpark. In the most unsurprising answer of his media session, Venable said he did not.</p><p>“I understand the rivalry, and it’s exciting to be a part of,” said Venable, a former Cubs coach. “But I don’t think there’s any animosity that I’m feeling or that I’m putting out there. I’m just excited to have an opportunity to play the Cubs.</p><p>“Being here with the Cubs, having seen that firsthand, being here with other teams and then being with the White Sox now, it’s a great place for a baseball game. And when the White Sox are here, obviously it is, even though it’s probably electric pretty much every day here.”</p><p>It certainly was during a back-and-forth game that saw the Cubs come out on top 7-5. Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong won it with a two-run homer against Sox rookie lefty Hagen Smith that scored automatic runner Carson Kelly leading off the 10th inning. </p><p>“It was a fun game to play,” said Venable, who chose not to walk Crow-Armstrong because he wanted the lefty-lefty matchup. “Obviously, outside of the result, when we were able to hear the White Sox fans in the crowd, there was a lot of White Sox presence there, which was really cool to see.” </p><p>With both teams on course for the postseason, that electricity crackled while the lineups were being announced, with a sizable portion of Sox fans making themselves heard. It continued when Sox relievers walked to their bullpen beneath the right-field bleachers in the middle of the first inning, with fans either cursing or saluting their arrival.</p><p>It reached a fever pitch when Crow-Armstrong — the target of a certain female Sox fan’s taunts in the series finale at Rate Field — stepped to the plate. Sox fans’ boos were audible, but they quickly became groans when the leadoff man sent Luis Castillo’s first-pitch fastball 376 feet into the bleachers in right.</p><p>When Seiya Suzuki sent Castillo’s fourth pitch, another fastball, 440 feet to center field, Sox fans might’ve felt their worst nightmare coming true. But Castillo settled in, and Sox fans tried to make the Friendly Confines as unfriendly to the Cubs as possible. </p><p>In the fourth inning, Wrigley Field turned into Rate Field North with chants of “Let’s go, White Sox!” And with two runners on, Randal Grichuk — who played for another Cubs rival, the Cardinals, in 2014-17 — responded with a 404-foot blast to center.</p><p>The momentum swings and accompanying crowd participation had been diminished in the crosstown rivalry while the Sox endured three consecutive seasons with more than 100 losses. But the players still felt something. This week, they’ll feel it more.</p><p>“In some sense it’s different,” said Sox right-hander Erick Fedde, who also pitched for the team in 2024, when it set the record for losses in a season with 121. “In ’24, I did feel like those were the biggest games for us because whether we’re out of the playoffs or not, it was a three-game set to give our fans pride.</p><p>“I still think that pride really matters and stands loudly in the sense of we want to put our foot down and play well and make our side of town feel like we’re winning the Chicago series. Big picture, we want to win to keep pressing for the playoffs. But this is still very important. I don't want to undersell it. entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker pours $65M into his campaign fund ahead of November elections
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has added $65 million to his gubernatorial campaign — giving him flexibility to spend on his own campaign and to support other candidates across the country.</p><p>The contribution was reported on Aug. 10, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections. Pritzker is heavily favored to win a third term in November, facing Republican challenger Darren Bailey, whom he beat in 2022. Prior to that large contribution, Pritzker had about $3.1 million cash on hand ahead of the November election. In the past, the billionaire governor has self-funded his three campaigns to the tune of more than $326 million since 2017.</p><p>While speculation is rampant about whether he will run for president in 2028, the Democratic governor cannot transfer funds from his state campaign fund to a federal campaign fund, should he choose to run. He can continue spending millions on ads for his gubernatorial run, send money to a PAC, a state party, county committees and ward committee organizations. He can also use the money to help support a Chicago mayoral candidate, although he has not yet publicly supported any of the declared candidates.</p><p>Pritzker helped out his longtime running mate Juliana Stratton in the U.S. Senate Democratic primary by contributing $10 million to the Illinois Future PAC, which allowed it to blast ads to support her and criticize her main opponent, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi. He has also given to Democratic Senate and House committees. In March, Pritzker gave $54,300 to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, who is running in the open Senate seat in North Carolina. He also gave $44,300.00 to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, according to the Federal Election Commission. </p><p>Pritzker's campaign declined to comment on the contribution on Monday night.<br></p>

entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong homers twice, joins 30-30 club and gives Cubs walk-off win vs. White Sox: ‘Pete’s my MVP’
entries.summary: <p>It’s <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong’s</b> world, and the rest of baseball is just living in it.</p><p>That’s how it has felt plenty of times during an MVP-caliber season by the Cubs’ center fielder, who put another big exclamation point on his award case Monday night by smacking a pair of home runs, the second of which resulted in a 7-5 walk-off victory in 10 innings over the crosstown-rival White Sox.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s blast sent him into the 30-30 club for a second consecutive season and gave the Cubs their 12th walk-off win of the season at Wrigley Field.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">PCA REACHES THE 30/30 MARK IN WALK-OFF FASHION. <a href="https://t.co/1JvfTLDk02">pic.twitter.com/1JvfTLDk02</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2089555460122677657?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“This is what great players do,” manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>said afterward. “We’ve got a number of these moments during the season from Pete. It’s a great-player moment. They step up in situations like this.”</p><p>The game was a back-and-forth classic between two teams with realistic playoff aspirations.</p><p></p><p>“It’s really frickin’ cool that we get to put that product out on the field together and go compete,” Crow-Armstrong said. “It’s really good for the city having both of us playing the kind of baseball we are and putting games out there like we did tonight.”</p><p></p><p>Crow-Armstrong started the scoring with the first of back-to-back homers in the first inning, with <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> delivering the other. In the fourth, Cubs starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b> gave up his 29th long ball of the season, a three-run shot by designated hitter <b>Randal Grichuk</b> that put the Sox in front, only for the Cubs to strike back the next inning, when they scored two on a tapped grounder and a throwing error.</p><p></p><p><b>Andrew Benintendi </b>smacked a game-flipping homer off Cubs trade-deadline addition <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> in the eighth, only for <b>Nico Hoerner </b>to tie the game in the bottom of the ninth ahead of Crow-Armstrong’s walk-off blast an inning later.</p><p></p><p>Add that shot to an ever-growing list of huge crosstown moments between the Cubs and Sox, this one big enough to stand out in a season full of them for Crow-Armstrong.</p><p></p><p>“I don’t think I’ve ever met a player like that,” Imanaga said through an interpreter. “You watch him play, make the fantastic plays that he does, and you’re not really surprised. But the expectations that you may have or a fan may have for him, he always surpasses it. It’s been incredible.”</p><p></p><p>“Pete’s my MVP,” said reliever <b>Jacob Webb</b> (5-2), who was credited with the win after throwing a scoreless 10th.</p><p></p><h3>Webb again</h3><p></p><p>Webb extended his streak of scoreless appearances to 22.</p><p></p><p>“He hasn’t been a guy that’s pitched in the ninth inning and pitched in these moments, and when you watch him pitch, it feels like he’s been out there for the last 10 years,” Counsell said. “That’s the feeling I get. There’s nobody I’d rather have out there. He continues to impress every time he gets the ball.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Slander against Black fathers is as old as our country
entries.summary: <p>Last week I had lunch with an old friend.</p><p>He is a Black Republican and a popular commentator, which means we have spent 20 years disagreeing in public and liking each other in private. He would be welcome in any barbershop in America. He keeps it real in the way men in any true community require of one another.</p><p>We talked about our kids. That was most of the lunch.</p><p>Nothing about that would surprise any Black man reading this. Nothing about it would surprise most Black people.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d20000" name="module-d20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>But every Black father carries something else around with him. We know the stereotypes: that we do not stay, that we do not provide, that we are not there.</p><p>Those stories are as old as the country itself.</p><p>So is the proof against them. And the proof was written down by the men who owned us.</p><p>In November of 1836, a man named Richard escaped near Morganton, North Carolina. He got away while the brother of the man who claimed him was hauling him to Alabama.</p><p>The enslaver bought newspaper space to get him back. His advertisement did not guess where Richard was headed. It told readers exactly where to look.</p><p>Richard had a wife, a free woman of color named Jane Tucker. She was arranging to return to Raleigh. The ad said there was no doubt her husband would try to get to her.</p><p>The man who owned Richard was not speculating. He put money behind it. He had seen enough men run toward a wife or a child to know where to send the search party. He expected his readers to know it too.</p><p>Historians have been collecting those advertisements for years. The Freedom on the Move project indexes close to 90,000. They name wives. They name children. They name the road the man was likely taking to reach them.</p><p>Capture meant brutal punishment. Escape itself could be deadly. They ran anyway.</p><p>They did not wait for the war to end, either.</p><p>On Dec. 27, 1862, Henry Christian placed a notice in a Philadelphia newspaper. He was searching for Richard, Rebecca and Rachel Christian. His children. Last known to be traveling out of Winchester, Virginia.</p><p>Historians at Villanova University have recovered nearly 5,000 notices like it. Freed people paying for newspaper space, year after year, hunting for family sold away. Judith Giesberg, who leads that project, estimates the success rate may have been as low as two in a hundred.</p><p>They kept paying anyway.</p><p>Many of those notices were placed by men. Fathers. Husbands. Brothers.</p><p>Herbert Gutman went through the records community by community. In the places he studied, most Black families had two parents in the house. In some rural areas it ran above eight in ten.</p><p>Now come forward to our own time.</p><p>Among fathers living with their small children, Black fathers were the most likely of the groups the study counted to bathe, dress and change them every day. Seventy percent did. For White fathers, 60%. For Hispanic fathers, 45%.</p><p>Among fathers of school-age children, 41% of Black fathers helped with homework or checked it daily. For White fathers, 28%.</p><p>That study covered 2006 to 2010. It is still the most recent we have, because the government stopped asking.</p><p>A later look at federal data, from 2017 to 2019, found the pattern holds for fathers living apart from their children. Nearly six in 10 Black fathers saw their children weekly. For White fathers, about four in 10.</p><p>That survey also has the hard number, and I will not skip it. Forty-three percent of Black fathers have at least one child living somewhere else. For White fathers it is 14.</p><p>That is not a shortage of men who want to father. Black fathers who live with their children are among the most involved in this country. The ones living apart report showing up more than anybody.</p><p>Something keeps pulling them out of the house.</p><p>Work left those neighborhoods. Violence rose. Prisons filled. Researchers have spent 40 years untangling how the three feed one another.</p><p>None of it is new. None of it is only ours. It hit Black neighborhoods first and hardest, then kept going until it reached everybody.</p><p>Next week I will show you those numbers. They belong to every man in America.</p><p>My friend and I did not talk about any of this over lunch. We talked about our kids.</p><p>That is what fathers do.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ae0000" name="module-ae0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Toxic Relationship Affects Woman's Health
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 54-year-old woman who, after 40 years, reconnected with my childhood best friend, "Neil." We are now engaged. I have no children, but Neil has two girls ages 11 and 13. The 11-year-old is in therapy and on medication for depression and anxiety. I love them as if they were my own. Their mother is useless and irresponsible, and Neil can't stand her.</p><p>My problem is that his behavior is not much better. Neil has severe anger issues. He has cursed at me and called me horrible names (in front of the girls) many times. Since we started couples therapy, he has improved, but he still displays anger issues, has a drinking problem and has no control over his children. They have no rules, discipline or any kind of parenting from him or their mother.</p><p>I am miserable and want to leave. We've been together almost five years, and I don't want to hurt him again. He'd be destroyed. Worse, the girls would be devastated. I'm scared about how the younger one would react. I would also be devastated.</p><p>I am bipolar, and my mental and emotional health have been severely affected. My physical health is also deteriorating because of so much stress — stomach issues, weight loss, psoriasis. My personal therapist is not much help. What do I do? — <i>OVER MY HEAD IN NEW YORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR OVER:</b> My first thought is that you should change therapists if this one isn't helpful. Then, after you regain some strength, stop worrying about Neil. You might find it helpful to attend some Al-Anon meetings. If you do, you will come to understand that his anger and alcohol issues aren't something you can solve by staying with him.</p><p>Neil's children are not and should not be your responsibility. If you haven't been able to establish a healthy, stable environment for them (at least when they are staying with their dad), accept that it isn't likely to happen. Explain to the children that it is not their fault that you are leaving, and then move on.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married for 26 years. I have often felt as if we were growing apart, often finding interests in different things. We seem unable to discuss our emotions without one of us getting hurt feelings and the talk devolving into awful arguments. There has never been any real question of extramarital affairs.</p><p>One night, I playfully asked if I could go through his computer. He immediately became defensive, saying he just doesn't like people getting into his computer, messing with his stuff. I get that. I wouldn't want just anybody getting into my computer, either. However, I am not just anybody; I'm his wife. He has full access to all of my computers, phones and digital accessories. Why do I feel like he's got something to hide? I don't know what to do. — <i>PRESUMPTION OF GUILT</i></p><p><b>DEAR PRESUMPTION:</b> Pressing your husband on this issue right now will only lead to more arguments. If you want to repair the marriage, you both need to learn to communicate more effectively. Without mentioning his computer, invite your husband to see a licensed family therapist with you. If he refuses, go without him. If he agrees, work on the basics now and save the privacy issues and your suspicions for future sessions.</p>

entries.title: Illinois lawmakers want chaotic 'mega master' hearings at Chicago’s immigration court to end
entries.summary: <p>Illinois' Democratic Congressional delegation is calling for the end of so-called “mega master” hearings that have packed immigration courts with chaos and led to record numbers of immigrants missing court and becoming targets for deportation.</p><p>U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi denounced the hearings as the “latest effort to weaponize the immigration courts to facilitate mass removals” at the expense of due process, in a five-page letter sent to Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday. The lawmakers repeatedly cited recent Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ reporting in the letter, which was signed by nearly every Illinois Democratic member of Congress.</p><p>At Chicago’s Downtown immigration court, Sun-Times and WBEZ reporters<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" > documented</a> daily schedules with as many as 185 cases per judge, tiny courtrooms holding dozens more people than they were designed for, and drastically shrinking notice time for immigrants to appear before a judge — with or without a lawyer.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" >Chaotic, crowded Chicago immigration mega court hearings are fueling record deportation orders</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“These so-called mega master hearings appear to be the latest example of policies prioritizing enforcement and deportation quotas over due process, while creating unnecessary fear, confusion, and uncertainty for the communities we represent,” the Illinois Democrats wrote to the Department of Justice, which oversees immigration court. “Immigration proceedings must prioritize fairness and the rule of law, rather than numerical enforcement targets.”</p><p>The lawmakers also asked for explanations for the reductions in notice time to appear in court and for guarantees of adequate personnel to handle the steep rise in cases.</p><p>“Immigrants have the right to have their case considered, but EOIR has made a mockery of due process in favor of meeting arbitrary deportation quotas,” Durbin said in an email, referring to the Executive Office of Immigration Review, the official name for immigration court. “These ‘mega master’ hearings must be put to an end.”</p><p>Krishnamoorthi said, “No one should be railroaded through a proceeding that could determine whether they remain in this country without adequate notice, access to legal counsel, or a real opportunity to make their case. Our letter demands the Administration end these mass hearings and uphold due process.”</p><p>But the letter sent to Blanche — confirmed recently as U.S. Attorney General after spending years as President Donald Trump’s personal criminal defense attorney — faces serious limits on what it can accomplish.</p><p>Trump’s party still controls both houses of Congress, where Republicans have shown an unwillingness to buck the will of the president who has long prioritized mass deportations. And the administration has not typically responded to such letters in the past.</p><p>DOJ officials have previously said in prepared statements that the amped up scheduling is meant to clear backlogs that left immigrants on dockets for years awaiting rulings.</p><p>In federal immigration court, “master hearings” are procedural hearings meant to inform non-citizens of their rights and responsibilities as they seek to prove why they should be allowed to stay in the United States.</p><p>But in late May, the usual groupings of 30 to 40 immigrants on a judge’s morning calendar ballooned upwards of 100. WBEZ and the Sun-Times showed that in June, for the first time since 2019, more immigrants missed court than appeared in the downtown Chicago courthouse, resulting in record orders for their removal in their absence.</p><p>Chicago stood out with the most mega hearings in June in its courthouse at 55 E. Monroe, as well as the most scheduled at the same time.<br></p>

entries.title: A 'black book' lists 34 people banned from Illinois casinos. It's rarely updated and likely missing names.
entries.summary: <p>After Chicago area bookie Vincent DelGiudice pleaded guilty in 2021 to running a sprawling illegal sports betting operation, the Orland Park resident was sentenced the following year to 18 months in prison.</p><p>He and his initial co-defendants, including Mettawa Mayor Casey Urlacher, later faced another penalty: They were banned by the Illinois Gaming Board, an arm of state government reporting to Gov. JB Pritzker, from ever stepping foot in an Illinois casino.</p><p>But the public could be forgiven if they didn’t know.</p><p>Even though the gaming board went through the process in late 2023 of permanently barring DelGiudice, along with nine others who were part of his case and two men who weren’t part of it, the agency did so with little or no fanfare, then left their names off its publicly available online “involuntary exclusion” list that identifies others similarly banned from Illinois casinos.</p><p>The gaming board’s administrator, Marcus Fruchter, won’t explain the omissions, declining to say whether they were purposeful or accidental.</p><p>An agency spokeswoman said in June, when the Chicago Sun-Times learned of them, that we “are not required by rule or law to display the names on the website” but are nonetheless “in the process of making updates to the website.”</p><p>That happened this past week, after the Sun-Times asked about the status of updates since it'd been two months. There are now 34 names displayed on the public list.</p><p>Beyond the latest additions, the 22 other exclusions spanned from 1993 to 2016.</p><p>Some of them were accused of being part of illegal gambling schemes — at times involving the mob, which has long claimed dominion over illicit gambling in Chicago and beyond, and has tried to make inroads into legal gambling.</p><p>Others were accused of cheating, stealing or creating havoc at casinos in Illinois or out of state. Two were accused of helping underage patrons visit casinos.</p><p>Created in the early 1990s as the state’s first casinos opened, the list has long served as a hall of shame of sorts that, among other things, is intended to serve as a deterrent for bad actors and a means for casinos to know who to keep out.</p><p>Among those already on the online public list:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-cf1dd4f2-972c-11f1-9ed3-437d5c997f26"><li>Robert Cechini, a one-time Bloomingdale resident convicted in an illegal video gambling case brought by authorities before video gambling was legalized in Illinois. He was added to the exclusion list in 2000.<br></li><li>James Dvorak, the former Cook County undersheriff convicted of corruption in the 1990s. He was added to the list in 2009 and says he’s aware of the banishment. “There’s nothing really you can do about it,” he said, adding it apparently had to do with “my alleged association with organized crime.” The restriction “didn’t really bother me.”<br></li><li>Christopher Rosario, who was involved in a 2007 fight in an Aurora casino and allegedly has “gang affiliation.”</li></ul><p>A certified letter sent by the gaming board to DelGiudice in December 2023 telling him he’s been forever banned from Illinois casinos says his “reputation and conduct” is such that his “presence within any Illinois casino gambling facility would jeopardize the safety, honesty, and integrity of the gambling operations.”</p><p>“This exclusion is PERMANENT.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Man who kicked a steer in the head at a suburban backyard rodeo is acquitted on an animal cruelty charge
entries.summary: <p>There doesn’t seem to be much debate over whether 68-year-old Socorro Barrientos repeatedly kicked a steer in the head last year at a backyard rodeo in the far northwest suburbs, which led to an animal cruelty charge against him.</p><p>Instead, in explaining a not guilty verdict rendered this past week in Barrientos’ case, McHenry County Judge Justin Hansen focused heavily on how the kicks landed and were delivered, with drone video showing the steer laying just outside the corral unable, or unwilling, to stand up as a foot came down 10 or more times.</p><p>While saying he “found this decision to be difficult” — and noting that Barrientos’ behavior was “perhaps not very kind” — Hansen said: “I do not find it to be cruel” through his analysis.</p><p>The defendant’s intent did not appear to be “to injure the cow or inflict pain or suffering,” Hansen said Thursday in a Woodstock courtroom. “I think he made an effort to move a cow back into the standing position.”</p><p>Hansen said Barrientos didn’t use the “tip of his boot” to kick the animal and “this action by the defendant appears to be one with little or no leverage.”</p><p>Had Barrientos been facing “the cow and stood with leverage on one foot and then reared back” as if he was “kicking a football,” that would’ve been “a very different maneuver,” Hansen said.</p><p>“There’s no indication the animal is affected or bothered” by what happened, as the “video does not show” the animal “expressing any reaction.”</p><p>Hansen also said of a veterinarian who had testified that the steer experienced “harm, fear and trauma” and endured “rough” kicks: “I think the doctor means well,” but he didn’t find her “to be particularly persuasive.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> baseline for what constitutes cruel treatment of an animal.”</p><p>“‘Cruel’ isn’t set in the statute.”</p><p>Nathan Noble, Barrientos’ attorney, said: “The judge made the right decision, it’s Sometimes the practice results in “degloving,” with the tails tearing away. The animals can be hurt in other ways — in some instances they suffer broken legs. </p><p>Those three men pleaded guilty, apologized and said they didn’t intend to hurt the steers.</p><p>A fifth person, a minor from Lockport, was initially cited but that case was later dropped.</p><p>All of the charges were based at least in part on drone video secretly taken by SHARK, which stands for Showing Animals Respect and Kindness and has been critical of Mexican-style and traditional American rodeos for years.</p><p>The Humane Care for Animals Act not only criminalizes direct mistreatment of pets and livestock, it also requires animal owners to provide “veterinary care when needed to prevent suffering.”</p><p>There’s been concern among some animal advocates that the law is too vague to consistently stop rodeo events such as steer tailing, so legislation has been proposed in the Illinois General Assembly and on the McHenry County Board to explicitly ban the practice.</p><p>Neither measure passed this year, but both legislative bodies are expected to discuss the subject again, though in McHenry County, board member Pam Althoff said that may involve proposed zoning restrictions.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/05/suburban-backyard-rodeos-steer-tailing-animal-cruelty" target="_blank" >Suburban backyard rodeos under fire, with steers knocked down, sometimes stripped of their tails</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Compared to other states, Illinois takes lax approach toward funeral home oversight
entries.summary: <p>The<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" > gruesome discovery</a> of unrefrigerated, decomposing bodies at a South Deering funeral home two weeks ago exposed the dearth of oversight over Illinois' funeral home industry. </p><p> Illinois is one of a mere handful of states that, absent complaints, do not conduct regular inspections of funeral homes, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://theconferenceonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Regulations-in-Licensing-2025-Finalized.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>2025 </u></a>survey from the International Conference of Funeral Service Examining Boards.</p><p>Illinois also is the only state that does not have a board or agency monitoring licensed funeral homes at their physical locations, the group said.</p><p>A recently signed law grants the state comptroller’s office more regulatory powers over cemeteries and crematories, but that purview doesn’t extend to funeral homes. The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation regulates funeral director and embalmer licenses.</p><p>“That kind of fragmentation cannot help this situation,” says Wake Forest University Law Professor Tanya Marsh, who teaches estate law, and studies laws surrounding the treatment and disposition of human remains.</p><p>What was found at the South Chicago Chapel funeral home earlier this month has prompted calls from elected officials for more reforms. State Rep. Marcus Evans, D-Chicago Heights, whose district includes the facility, called the situation “horrific” and said the legislature should have been “more proactive” in regulating the funeral home industry.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1a0000" name="image-1a0000"></a> <picture Marcus Evans in 2021. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has questioned who should investigate funeral homes given that his administration now only licenses the facilities, but he has said little else about what kind of legislative response should follow the horrors discovered at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>Marsh said the solution typically thrown around in the wake of grisly incidents such as the one in the South Chicago Chapel is to pass stronger licensing laws, limiting who comes into the profession in the first place.</p><p>But bad actors, she said, are often already licensed. While the state had revoked South Chicago Chapel owner Clark Morgan’s license in 2024, his wife Johanna had retained her license.</p><p>“If we can't figure out how to head off people from engaging in this kind of behavior, then we have to have some sort of enforcement mechanism on the back end to try and figure it out before it's too late,” Marsh said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" >Potential class-action lawsuit filed against South Deering funeral home for mishandling 56 bodies</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Michael D. Sharkey, an attorney who represents the Illinois Funeral Directors Association, said the group welcomes “fair and thoughtful regulation of funeral service.”</p><p>“Illinois has a lot of rules and regulations on the books concerning funeral homes and crematories,” Sharkey said. “[At South Chicago Chapel], I believe that this is a failure of state agencies to properly enforce those and to properly track the alleged nefarious characters.”</p><h3>Pritzker hints at oversight changes</h3><p>The state Department of Financial and Professional Regulation said it received a tip about “potential operation concerns” at the South Chicago Chapel, prompting Chicago police to investigate and uncover more than 50 unrefrigerated bodies at various stages of decomposition.</p><p>Prior to that tip, what had been going on at the funeral home had gone unnoticed by the state.</p><p>But some elected officials, including Pritzker, are questioning whether the state Department of Financial and Professional Regulation is the right avenue to handle complaints of potential abuses. The governor said he’s meeting with Comptroller Susana Mendoza’s office about possibly streamlining how complaints are reported to the state.</p><p>“IDFPR is a licensing organization, but the investigatory endeavor — we should all discuss whether that's something that should belong to IDFPR or to some other body,” Pritzker said.</p><p> On Monday, WBEZ sought clarity from Pritzker’s office on that comment and asked whether the governor favored regular funeral home inspections by the state, tougher criminal penalties for desecrating human remains inside funeral homes or creation of a blue-ribbon panel to propose tougher oversight measures for funeral homes.</p><p>A Pritzker spokesperson declined comment.</p><p>Thirty-six other states have created separate funeral boards to manage director licenses, funeral homes, crematories and cemeteries. The other 14 states, excluding Illinois, have appointed state agencies, such as public health departments, to the task.</p><p>Creating a unified board is something state Rep. Diane Blair-Sherlock, D-Villa Park, is considering. She chairs the House State Government Administration Committee, which typically handles funeral home legislation, and worked on the bill granting the comptroller more regulatory powers over cemeteries.</p><p>But Blair-Sherlock said she’s not sure if the comptroller or the IDFPR have the resources to become the state’s one-stop-shop for funeral industry oversight.</p><p>“Sometimes we want to give it to a department, and the department says we're not equipped for that,” Blair Sherlock said. “I believe that we will be able to do something early next year.”</p><p>And while a vast majority of other states carry out annual or bi-annual inspections of funeral homes, sometimes even unannounced searches, Illinois is one of four states — along with Alaska, Hawaii and Iowa — that do not conduct any inspections of licensed funeral homes, crematories or cemeteries.</p><p>Starting next year, the comptroller’s office will have authority to inspect cemeteries only after a complaint has been filed.</p><p>“The tragic situation that happened in Chicago, this is not a number of bodies that piled up in the last week, right?” Marsh said. “The more frequent inspections are by the state, the more likely they are to catch this kind of problem before it gets completely out of hand.”</p><p>A spokeswoman for Mendoza said she is also looking at implementing harsher criminal penalties for funeral directors who mishandle human remains following what happened at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>“Comptroller Mendoza believes these people belong in jail,” Mendoza spokeswoman Kim Howard said.</p><p> In 2024, Pritzker signed legislation that imposed new criminal penalties against funeral home operators who knowingly made false statements on death certificates, kept false records or maintained ill-equipped preparation rooms where bodies are prepared for burial.</p><p>There was no language in that law that explicitly imposed criminal penalties for the desecration of bodies inside funeral homes.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-mendoza-permanently-closes-heights-crematory-through-consent-order" target="_blank" ><u>In June 2025</u></a>, Mendoza’s office revoked the chapel’s crematory license, and handed over evidence of the owners improperly storing remains to the Cook County State’s Attorney's office and the Illinois State Police. Neither Clark nor Johanna Morgan were arrested.</p><p>Howard said the goal is to introduce legislation with tougher criminal penalties for funeral home operators during the fall veto session, which begins in mid-November.</p><h3><b>Lawmaker says state ‘not on top of this’</b></h3><p>Illinois has seen high-profile cases of funeral and cemetery directors mishandling human remains over the past 15 years.</p><p>In 2024, a downstate funeral home was found by authorities to have misidentified up to 800 cremated ashes. That triggered passage of a law requiring crematories to affix remains with a unique ID and maintain chain-of-custody documentation.</p><p>And in 2009, the Cook County Sheriff’s office found former Burr Oak Cemetery manager Carolyn Towns and three other workers had dug up graves, dumped the bodies and resold plots. The workers were later convicted, and Towns got a 12-year prison sentence.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7e0000" name="image-7e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e26e64/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c1749a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f369233/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rows of tombstones at the Burr Oak Cemetery in 2009. Evans is joining Blair-Sherlock and other Democratic members in calling for new legislation that would consolidate oversight of funeral homes and cemeteries under one state body. entries.summary: <p>The largest development project in Niles is transforming what was once a mecca for Chicago’s Polish community into hundreds of new units of housing.</p><p>Village officials said the Riverbank, a 10-building residential project at the former White Eagle Events and Convention Center, is expected to finish December 2027.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2016/09/18/the-making-of-polish-chicago" target="_blank" >White Eagle</a> — which cost $250,000 to demolish — was a staple among Polish families for funeral receptions, baptisms and other gatherings. The venue, 6839 N. Milwaukee Ave., hosted dignitaries spanning from former President Jimmy Carter to Pope John Paul II and Muhammad Ali. Poland's former President Lech Wałęsa also visited the White Eagle. be revitalized with art, much-needed housing and public green space.</p><p>“What you’re going to see along Milwaukee Avenue is transformation,” Chris Ragusto, Niles’ director of community development, said.</p><p>Developing the Riverbank is Noah Properties, led by Bart Przyjemski. Przyjemski is a native of Poland and a former Niles resident. He purchased the site in December 2025 for $5.7 million, with a $3.9 million mortgage from California-based Genesis Capital, property records show.</p><p>The Riverbank will have 354 luxury units including studios, one-, two- and four-bedroom homes. Pricing hasn't been determined. The site, spanning 7 acres, will also have a new park, public plaza, pool, playground and parking.</p><p>Construction has been ongoing for the past six months, according to village officials. In July, developers hit a major milestone: framing for the six rows of townhomes was completed. Some of the first townhomes have their windows installed, with interior finishes underway. By the end of August, crews will begin installing drywall, tile and flooring in some of the first units.</p><p>Steel framing is going up on one the apartment buildings, while a second apartment building has its foundation for the attached parking garage poured.</p><p>And where the White Eagle used to sit is a giant excavated hole, at least until construction starts at that portion of the site. The developer is still waiting on permit approvals for buildings planned at the front of the property. The medical building at 6759 N. Milwaukee has been vacated, and it will eventually be demolished.</p><p>Niles Mayor George Alpogianis said the Riverbank will help usher in the next chapter for the site. The apartments and townhomes will attract young professionals and families, who may not be ready or have the money to buy a home yet, but still want to be in Niles for its location, schools and public Ted Przybylo opened the business in 1947 and moved it from Chicago to Niles in 1967.</p><p>The White Eagle’s nearly 60-year run was “so monumental” for Niles and those who frequented it, including much of Chicago’s Democratic Party, Alpogianis said. But there’s no longer a need for a roughly 1,000-seat banquet hall like the White Eagle.</p><p>“As much as we worked with [the owners] to try and figure things out and try to reimagine the White Eagle, it unfortunately had its day,” Alpogianis said.</p><p>The White Eagle site is one the village “wanted to pay particular attention to,” Ragusto said. </p><p>Niles' South Milwaukee Avenue Corridor Plan calls for widening Milwaukee Avenue, which Noah Properties will undertake along with new landscaping and an art plaza. The 2040 plan also envisions Milwaukee Avenue as a place where residents can live, work, shop and play.</p><p>Remembering the history of the White Eagle is important as the Milwaukee Avenue parcel evolves, officials said.</p><p>The Niles Historical Society took a “number of items” from the banquet hall prior to demolition, Katie Schneider, deputy village manager of Niles, said. The items will likely be housed at The Niles Historical and Cultural Center, where they will help tell the story of Polish immigrants in the village. entries.title: ESPN co-founder Bill Rasmussen dies at 93 from the effects of Parkinson’s disease
entries.summary: <p>LAND O’ LAKES, Fla. (AP) — Bill Rasmussen, who co-founded ESPN in 1979 after being fired from a public relations job in the World Hockey Association, died Tuesday. He was 93.</p><p>ESPN historian Mike Soltys said Rasmussen died at his Florida home from the effects of Parkinson’s disease. Rasmussen announced in 2019 that he had been diagnosed with the degenerative disease in 2014.</p><p>“Bill was a remarkable man — a visionary and an innovator who conceived the idea of a network entirely devoted to sports,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “Quite simply, none of us would be here today if it wasn’t for Bill’s passion and all the hard work and entrepreneurial spirit he put into building ESPN in the late 1970s — key aspects of our company culture that still carry on to this day.”</p><p>Rasmussen and his son Scott came up with the idea of a network carrying sports around the clock, and it would revolutionize Americans’ TV-watching habits. But the pair didn’t stick around long. They were forced out after only a year by ESPN majority owner Getty Oil.</p><p>Bill Rasmussen’s original idea was a cable channel covering only Connecticut sports. Many cable operators in the state were skeptical, but someone suggested buying satellite time to reach a national audience.</p><p>ESPN was launched on Sept. 7, 1979. George Grande welcomed viewers to the first “SportsCenter” broadcast before the network’s first live event, a slow-pitch softball game between the Kentucky Bourbons and the Milwaukee Schlitz.</p><p>“In those days, we didn’t know if we’d last four weeks, four years, let alone 40-some, but we knew it was special,” Grande said. “Bottom line was Bill Rasmussen was the true pervader of the original American dream, and he gave us all something very special that we still have today.”</p><p>The Rasmussens secured financial backing from Getty Oil and a rights deal with the NCAA, and built a studio in Bristol, Connecticut, still under construction when ESPN went on the air.</p><p>The Getty investment and the deal with the NCAA occurred on the same day.</p><p>“When someone tells you you can’t do something, you want to prove them wrong,” Bill Rasmussen said. “Many, many people told us there wasn’t enough sports to do a 24-hour channel. I didn’t argue with anybody. I just thought they were wrong and I was right.”</p><p>When the Rasmussens were forced out of ESPN in 1980, Getty owned 85% of the network. Texaco, which had acquired Getty, sold its interest in ESPN to ABC in 1984.</p><p>Bill Rasmussen and ESPN were estranged until 1999, when company executives invited him to the 20th anniversary celebration. Since then, he has been embraced and recognized for his vision of creating an all-sports network. He toured the country in 2019 for the 40th anniversary and gave speeches at Walt Disney Co. and ESPN events.</p><p>“Bill was our George Washington and a good friend,” said veteran anchor Chris Berman, who joined ESPN three weeks after the network launched in 1979. “He was such a grateful person and every sports fan can be grateful for Bill. He wasn’t a glass half-full guy; his glass was always overflowing with optimism. He greeted everyone with a smile and we can all smile knowing Bill’s legacy.”</p><p>Born in Chicago, Rasmussen earned degrees from DePauw University in Indiana and Rutgers University and served in the Air Force. He started an advertising services business, then worked in radio and television as a broadcaster during the 1960s.</p><p>He was hired in 1974 as public relations director for the WHA’s New England Whalers in Hartford, Connecticut. The team’s entire front office was fired in 1978, and Rasmussen soon turned his attention to brainstorming with his son on the creation of sports on cable TV with the help of a $9,000 credit card advance.</p><p>“There was a whole lot of chutzpah and a whole lot of vision, and they’re maxed out on their credit cards. It’s the American dream,” said Bob Ley, one of the network’s original anchors.</p><p>Rasmussen was inducted into the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame in 2025.</p><p>Rasmussen was predeceased by his wife of 56 years, Lois, in 2011 and is survived by two sons, Scott Rasmussen and his wife, Laura, and Glenn Rasmussen, daughter Lynn Van Hollebeke and her husband, Louie, seven grandchildren, one great-grandson and one great-granddaughter. In addition to his wife, Bill was predeceased by his brothers Robert and Donald Rasmussen, sister Vivien and a grandson.</p>

entries.title: Pumpkins, pensions, and the CTU's 'cooked' books
entries.summary: <p>Is criticism a crime?</p><p>As fond as I am of teachers, generally, and despite being a good union man myself, I couldn't help but shake my head in wonder at the Chicago Teachers Union, which I consider a fairly savvy organization, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/17/chicago-teachers-union-illinois-policy-institute-defamation-lawsuit-stacy-davis-gates" >suing a pair of conservative watchdogs,</a> the Illinois Policy Institute and the Liberty Justice Center, for sinking their teeth into CTU finances and accusing the union of using "cooked" books.</p><p>First, way to turn a spotlight on their accusations. Believe it or not, I'm not checking the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/illinois-grows-enough-pumpkins-for-8b-pumpkin-spice-lattes/" target="_blank" >Illinois Policy Institute website</a> every morning to see what's in their crosshairs. Doing that, right now, I see their top story is on ... pumpkins. "The state produces enough pumpkins to make nearly 8 billion pumpkin spice lattes, the most pumpkins in the U.S." At first I thought it must be a mistake — the colorful, pumpkin-centric page labeled "Illinois Policy" must be different from "Illinois Policy Institute."</p><p>Nope. Same folks.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fd0000" name="module-fd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>But is it true? <a class="Link" href="https://www.blogger.com/blog/post/edit/3972382144120426476/4857837068088532900#" target="_blank" >According to the United States Department of Agriculture</a>, the top producer of pumpkins in the country is ... Illinois, head and shoulders above the rest, responsible for 40% of all the big orange squashes grown nationwide.</p><p>Did you know that? I did not. Score one for the Illinois Policy Institute.</p><p>The second story "CHICAGO TEACHERS UNION UNDERMINES YET ANOTHER CHARTER SCHOOL" begins: "The Chicago Teachers Union’s relentless attacks on charter schools has claimed another victim. The Chicago High School for the Arts announced it will not renew its contract with Chicago Public Schools, citing financial struggles. It will stop operations at the end of the current 2025-2026 school year."</p><p>Is that true? Kinda. The charter school will stop operations, but the school itself will transition into a public school. You could also say ... as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/07/30/chiarts-funding-vote-postponed-as-cps-board-debates-budget-consequences" target="_blank" >a Sun-Times story</a> suggested last month ... that CPS stepped in and saved the school after its charter operators decided to abandon it, one of the many downsides of privatizing public education. As a rule, the Chicago Public Schools are not shutting down schools willy-nilly, at least not since Rahm Emanuel left office.</p><p>That said, with Republicans dwelling in a near hallucinatory fantasy world where elections they lose are by definition fraudulent and along with inconvenient timbers of the Constitution can simply be wished away, I'd say that any thinking that bears even a rough resemblance to reality ought to be encouraged. So yes, just as the teachers union is opposed to charter schools, viewing them as corporate dodges to get around union protections, so the IPI is for them, as part of the parental choice/school voucher canard designed to direct public money into private pockets. Let the best man win.</p><p></p><p>Spin aside, I'm learning stuff. Honestly, quite an attractive website. I'll have to add it to my list.</p><p>The third story, "WITHOUT REFORMS, PENSION INSOLVENCY WILL EAT CHICAGO ALIVE," well, hard to argue that one. I've said for years that the city slides toward becoming one vast pension fund that also puts out fires. Maybe the CTU will sue me next.</p><p>Not to give them ideas. Back to suing Illinois Policy Institute. Bush league move. Did the CTU ever pause to wonder how this makes them look? Spend any time communicating in public and people are going to attack you. If I sued everyone who accused me of simply parroting whatever George Soros instructs me to say, I'd spend all my time in court.</p><p>Speaking of court. Since the lawsuit pivots on charges that the CTU "cooked" their books, doesn't this lawsuit invite the Illinois Policy Institute to pick over the union's finances with a lice comb, and show up in court with all sorts of charts highlighting every error, discrepancy and questionable meal expense they can find? Isn't that exactly what the IPI wants to do anyway? And isn't the CTU basically shining klieg lights, setting the stage for the IPI to parade their charges and theories across? I think they are.</p><p>In checking out the Illinois Policy Institute's reputation, I found a 2018 article that says this about the organization:</p><p>"Its studies and opinion pieces on cutting government spending and boosting transparency became must-read material to many Republicans, some Democrats," Mick Dumke and Tina Sfondeles wrote in the Sun-Times, while pointing out that its operator, John Tillman, was raking in millions.</p><p>"As the institute attacked political insiders for profiting off the system, Tillman parlayed its small-government message into growing paychecks for himself and other top staff members, tax filings and audits show," the paper wrote.</p><p>Though the story questioned the legality of what the Illinois Policy Institute was doing, its leaders did not sue the Sun-Times. What do they know that the Chicago Teachers Union doesn't?</p>

entries.title: Bears coach: RB Kyle Monangai 'week-to-week' after hurting knee
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-training-camp-kyle-monangai-right-knee-injury-practice" target="_blank" >Kyle Monangai</a> seems to have avoided the worst-case scenario.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson said Tuesday that he will be "week-to-week" with a knee injury that he suffered Sunday when he got tangled up with defensive tackle Grady Jarrett during a drill in which neither of them were wearing full pads. </p><p>The injury could have been much worse. Monangai limped off the field and Jarrett was emotional about the collision.</p><p>Johnson said Tuesday that he didn't need to have a conversation with Jarrett, who is entering his 12th season in the NFL and second with the Bears.</p><p>Roschon Johnson and Salvon Ahmed had been behind Monangai during training camp and figure to get the majority of his work in the weeks moving forward. Johnson led the team in carries and rushing yards Saturday against the Browns, while Ahmed scored on a 49-yard screen pass.</p><p>The Bears' season opener is more than 3 1/2 weeks away.</p><p></p>
